investigation.title: Remote Agent Pod Scheduling Failure: Exhausted kata.peerpods.io/vm Capacity Across All Available Nodes
investigation.summary: All three remote-agent checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) failed in production-api because the Kubernetes scheduler could not place the agent pod: 2 nodes reported Insufficient kata.peerpods.io/vm capacity and the remaining 4 nodes did not match the pod's node affinity or selector. The pod remained unscheduled for 138–143 seconds before the eval timeout was reached, producing empty evidence and failing all contract assertions.
investigation.rootCause: The Kubernetes cluster backing the remote-agent swarm has exhausted its kata.peerpods.io/vm resource on the 2 nodes that carry that resource class. The remaining 4 nodes are excluded by the pod's node affinity or selector rules. With no schedulable node and no preemption victims available, every remote-agent pod creation attempt times out before reaching a running/idle/ready state. This is a cluster-capacity or node-affinity configuration problem in the production-api runtime environment, not an eval infrastructure defect. No evidence of a user-traffic or incident signal is present; the impact is scoped to the AURA observability eval for the remote-agents feature.

source-context.infra/evals/status/check-expectations.json:250-258: contract requires vmIdPresent=true and remoteState oneOf [running, idle, ready]; neither assertion can be evaluated because the pod never started.
possibleCauses: PRIMARY — kata.peerpods.io/vm resource exhaustion on the 2 eligible nodes: all available VM slots on the kata peer-pods nodes are occupied by existing workloads, leaving no capacity for a new remote-agent pod. This is directly stated in the scheduler message (failed-check.message).

SECONDARY — Node affinity or selector misconfiguration: the pod's affinity/selector rules restrict scheduling to only the 2 kata-capable nodes, and those nodes are full. If the selector were broadened or additional kata-capable nodes were added, scheduling could succeed.

TERTIARY — Insufficient cluster scale-out: the cluster has only 6 nodes total, 4 of which are ineligible by affinity, and the 2 eligible nodes have no remaining kata.peerpods.io/vm quota. A cluster autoscaler may not be configured or may not have triggered in time.
LOWER — Transient spike in concurrent remote-agent workloads consuming all VM slots at the time of the eval run, which would be a temporary rather than structural capacity problem.

recommendedNextActions: Immediately check the kata.peerpods.io/vm node capacity in the production-api cluster to determine whether VM slots are fully consumed and by which workloads.
If slots are exhausted by long-running or leaked remote-agent VMs, identify and terminate stale VMs to free capacity for new scheduling attempts.
If the cluster is structurally under-provisioned, add additional kata peer-pods capable nodes or increase the kata.peerpods.io/vm quota on existing nodes.
Review the pod's node affinity and selector rules to determine whether the restriction to 2 nodes is intentional; if not, correct the selector to allow scheduling on additional eligible nodes.
After restoring capacity, re-run all three remote-agent eval probes (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) to confirm the feature returns to a passing state.
Consider adding a cluster-level alert on kata.peerpods.io/vm utilization approaching 100% so capacity exhaustion is detected before it causes eval or provisioning failures.

whatWouldDisproveThis: If the kata.peerpods.io/vm nodes show available (unallocated) VM capacity at the time of the failure, resource exhaustion is not the cause and a different scheduler or admission error should be investigated.

If the pod spec's node affinity or selector is found to be misconfigured (e.g., targeting a non-existent label), the root cause would shift from capacity exhaustion to a configuration error independent of actual VM slot availability.

If a subsequent eval run immediately after this failure succeeds without any cluster changes, the failure was transient (e.g., a concurrent workload released VM slots), not a structural capacity problem.

If the 4 non-kata nodes are shown to also carry the kata.peerpods.io/vm resource but the pod's selector excludes them incorrectly, the root cause would be a selector misconfiguration rather than true capacity exhaustion.

If the eval runner itself is shown to have thrown an exception before reaching the createAgent() call (e.g., requireOrgId failing), the scheduler message would be a secondary artifact and the primary cause would be an auth or org-resolution failure.
followUpEvals: Add a dedicated eval that probes kata.peerpods.io/vm node capacity directly (e.g., checks that at least N VM slots are allocatable across the cluster) to catch exhaustion before it blocks agent creation.

Add a pre-flight scheduling check eval that submits a dry-run pod (using kubectl --dry-run=server) with the remote-agent spec and asserts it is schedulable, providing earlier signal than waiting for a full agent creation timeout.

Add a remote-agent VM slot headroom eval that asserts the ratio of used-to-allocatable kata.peerpods.io/vm slots stays below a configurable threshold (e.g., 80%), enabling a warning before full exhaustion.

Consider splitting the remote-agent-create eval into two stages: (1) pod schedulability assertion and (2) VM readiness assertion, so scheduling failures are distinguished from VM boot or runtime failures in future reports.

investigation.title: Remote Agent Pod Scheduling Failure: Exhausted kata.peerpods.io/vm Capacity Blocks All Remote Agent Checks
investigation.summary: All three remote-agents feature checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) failed in production-api at 2026-07-17T03:28–03:33Z with an identical Kubernetes scheduling error: the cluster's 6 nodes had zero schedulable capacity for kata.peerpods.io/vm pods, with 2 nodes reporting insufficient VM quota and 4 nodes rejecting the pod due to node affinity/selector mismatch. Because no remote agent pod could be scheduled, the eval runner's createAgent call never completed, leaving all required evidence fields (orgId, agentId, readyState, state) unpopulated and causing the remote-agent-state contract validation to fail entirely.
investigation.rootCause: The Kubernetes cluster backing the production-api remote-agents feature has exhausted its kata.peerpods.io/vm resource quota on the 2 nodes that match the pod's affinity/selector requirements. With 0 of 6 nodes available for scheduling and preemption unable to free capacity, the eval runner's attempt to create a remote agent pod timed out after ~143 seconds. This is an infrastructure-layer scheduling failure that prevented the eval from reaching any application logic, so no evidence (orgId, agentId, readyState, state) was ever written. This is an eval-layer signal of a real infrastructure constraint; no user-traffic or incident signals are present in the supplied evidence to confirm a broader production outage.

investigations.title: Remote Agent Pod Scheduling Failure: Exhausted kata.peerpods.io/vm Capacity Across All Available Nodes
investigations.summary: All three remote-agent checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) failed in production-api because the Kubernetes scheduler could not place the agent pod: 2 nodes reported Insufficient kata.peerpods.io/vm capacity and the remaining 4 nodes did not match the pod's node affinity or selector. The pod remained unscheduled for 138–143 seconds before the eval timeout was reached, producing empty evidence and failing all contract assertions.
investigations.rootCause: The Kubernetes cluster backing the remote-agent swarm has exhausted its kata.peerpods.io/vm resource on the 2 nodes that carry that resource class. The remaining 4 nodes are excluded by the pod's node affinity or selector rules. With no schedulable node and no preemption victims available, every remote-agent pod creation attempt times out before reaching a running/idle/ready state. This is a cluster-capacity or node-affinity configuration problem in the production-api runtime environment, not an eval infrastructure defect. No evidence of a user-traffic or incident signal is present; the impact is scoped to the AURA observability eval for the remote-agents feature.

possibleCauses: PRIMARY — kata.peerpods.io/vm resource exhaustion on the 2 eligible nodes: all available VM slots on the kata peer-pods nodes are occupied by existing workloads, leaving no capacity for a new remote-agent pod. This is directly stated in the scheduler message (failed-check.message).

SECONDARY — Node affinity or selector misconfiguration: the pod's affinity/selector rules restrict scheduling to only the 2 kata-capable nodes, and those nodes are full. If the selector were broadened or additional kata-capable nodes were added, scheduling could succeed.

TERTIARY — Insufficient cluster scale-out: the cluster has only 6 nodes total, 4 of which are ineligible by affinity, and the 2 eligible nodes have no remaining kata.peerpods.io/vm quota. A cluster autoscaler may not be configured or may not have triggered in time.
LOWER — Transient spike in concurrent remote-agent workloads consuming all VM slots at the time of the eval run, which would be a temporary rather than structural capacity problem.

Consider splitting the remote-agent-create eval into two stages: (1) pod schedulability assertion and (2) VM readiness assertion, so scheduling failures are distinguished from VM boot or runtime failures in future reports.

possibleCauses: Primary — kata.peerpods.io/vm resource exhaustion on the 2 eligible nodes: concurrent workloads or prior eval runs have consumed all available VM slots, leaving none for the eval-triggered pods. This is directly stated in the scheduler message (failed-check.message).

Secondary — node affinity/selector mismatch on 4 of 6 nodes: the remote-agent pod spec requires a node label or taint that only 2 nodes satisfy, reducing the schedulable pool to those 2 already-exhausted nodes. Even if VM capacity were partially freed, the affinity constraint limits recovery to those same 2 nodes.

Tertiary — cluster under-provisioned for concurrent eval load: if multiple eval runs or production workloads compete for the same 2 kata.peerpods.io nodes simultaneously, transient exhaustion would cause sporadic eval failures without a persistent infrastructure problem.

Lower confidence — eval runner does not implement a retry or back-off before declaring failure: the probe timed out at ~150 s with no retry, so a brief transient capacity spike would produce the same failure signal as a sustained outage.

whatWouldDisproveThis: A passing re-run of remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, or remote-agent-runtime with full evidence (orgId, agentId, model, provider, message) returned would show the scheduling problem was transient and has self-resolved.
kubectl describe nodes showing kata.peerpods.io/vm allocatable capacity greater than currently allocated on the 2 eligible nodes would disprove sustained exhaustion and point to a transient spike.

A scheduler event on the pending pod showing a different failure reason (e.g., image pull error, resource quota, network policy) would indicate the kata.peerpods.io/vm message was a secondary symptom rather than the primary cause.

Evidence that the 4 affinity-excluded nodes were intentionally excluded by design and the 2 eligible nodes have free VM slots would shift the diagnosis toward a different scheduling constraint or a bug in the pod spec.

A passing run of the local-agent-create or local-agent-runtime checks (which do not use kata.peerpods.io VMs) at the same time would confirm the failure is isolated to the remote/kata VM layer and not a broader cluster or API failure.
followUpEvals: Add a dedicated eval check that directly queries kata.peerpods.io/vm node capacity (allocatable vs. allocated) and fails with a warning before exhaustion reaches 100%, enabling proactive alerting ahead of scheduling failures.

Add a node-affinity coverage eval that verifies at least N nodes satisfy the remote-agent pod's affinity/selector requirements, catching misconfigurations that reduce the schedulable pool below a safe threshold.

Consider splitting the remote-agent-create eval into two stages: (1) pod scheduling success and (2) agent readiness, so scheduling failures are reported as a distinct signal from agent runtime failures.
Add a concurrent-capacity eval that tracks how many remote-agent VM slots are in use at eval run time, providing context for interpreting scheduling failures as capacity vs. configuration issues.
